claims.text: Switching from continuous-wave high-thermal-load melting to ultrashort-pulse laser additive manufacturing will reduce residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Ultrashort-pulse laser additive manufacturing will limit microstructural degradation in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Ultrashort-pulse laser additive manufacturing will improve the mechanical performance of AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
The starting AlCrFeNiSi powder is virgin and in an as-sieved state.
Sub-picosecond laser pulses provide highly localized, minimal thermal input during melting.
The proposed processing window is for components smaller than 10 mm fabricated under high vacuum with controlled energy input and modest substrate preheating.
Ultrashort-pulse processing will produce a refined microstructure with limited grain growth and suppressed coarsening.
The refined microstructure will mediate lower residual stress.
Ultrashort-pulse processing will produce a more uniform distribution of phases.
Ultrashort pulses cause melting and solidification to occur rapidly within a confined thermal zone.
A confined thermal zone minimizes heat diffusion into surrounding material.
Localized rapid solidification leads to a finer microstructure.
Localized rapid solidification causes less accumulation of thermal stress than conventional high-thermal-load processing.
Ultrashort-pulse processed parts will have higher yield strength than parts made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
Ultrashort-pulse processed parts will have greater ductility than parts made under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
Ultrashort-pulse processing will reduce the complexity of thermal management.
Conventional continuous-wave or long-pulse laser additive manufacturing inherently produces higher thermal loads and larger heat-affected zones.
The hypothesis is primarily applicable to sub-10 mm components fabricated under high-vacuum conditions.
Scalability of the ultrashort-pulse setup and the absorption characteristics of AlCrFeNiSi may limit applicability.
